newsitem.title: USA: Clinton stresses economy on final campaign swing.
newsitem.headline: Clinton stresses economy on final campaign swing.

text.p: President Bill Clinton, on his final campaign swing, on Wednesday promoted the opportunities created by his economic policies -- a message that won him the White House four years ago and appears likely to keep him there now.

Leaving Washington for the final campaign swing before Election Day on Tuesday, Clinton used an appearance at Eastern Michigan University to take on Republican rival Bob Dole's claim that the nation's economy has been weak -- despite a rise in consumer confidence.
"Our economy is continuing to grow steady and strong," Clinton said, citing the improved state of the economy since he took office in 1993 and the benefits it has generated, particularly for women.

The Commerce Department on Wednesday said the nation's gross domestic product expanded at a 2.2 percent annual rate from July through September, less than half the robust 4.7 percent pace that had been posted during the second quarter.

Although administration officials tried to play down the slowdown -- which Wall Street had feared could have been as low as 1.8 percent -- Dole's campaign quickly cited it as proof that the economy was not as strong as most Americans seem to think.

"The myth of the Clinton recovery has long been known to anxious wage-earners and now the cold statistics Bill Clinton is so fond of are falling, too," said Nelson Warfield, the Dole campaign's press secretary.
Dole, who advocates an across the board 15 percent income tax cut, has centred his campaign on an economic package he says is necessary to revive economic growth.

Clinton, clearly enjoying his frontrunner status, said he was "a little amused" that Dole earlier in the day "said that we had the worst economy in 20 years. Now two weeks ago he said it was the worst enonomy in 100 years, so we're making progress."

With less than a week remaining in the campaign, the Republican challenger's economic plan has generated only limited support. The latest Reuters tracking poll shows Clinton ahead of Dole by 9.8 percentage points.
Dole, in a bid to revive his fortunes, has been attacking Democrats for accepting political contributions from financial interests in Indonesia and elsewhere in Asia.

An embarrassed Democratic Party tried to defuse an uproar when it initially announced it would not file a report to the Federal Election Commission on contributions and expenditures for the first two weeks of October. Republicans threatened to seek a federal court injunction to freeze all Democratic spending but Connecticut Sen. Christopher Dodd, the Democratic Party chairman, said all documents will be released soon.
Clinton aides said he planned to address campaign financing in a speech on Friday in California, castigating Dole and House Speaker Newt Gingrich for standing in the way of previous reform efforts.

Dole once sentenced a campaign finance bill to death with a filibuster -- a tactic in Congress that dooms proposals by threatening to speak endlessly -- and Gingrich agreed in a handshake with Clinton to reform campaign finance laws but no changes were enacted.
Clinton was to campaign in Colorado late on Wednesday before going to Arizona to spend the night. Since Sunday, he will have visited at least 21 states by Election Day.
